title: Refraction and lateral deviation of a beam through a glass slab
objective: To trace a ray of light through a rectangular glass slab and observe how it bends.
To measure the lateral displacement of the emergent beam.
To show that the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.
To find the refractive index of the glass from the angles of incidence and refraction.

theory.statement: A ray entering a glass slab obliquely is bent towards the normal, travels across the glass in a straight line, and is bent away from the normal by exactly the same amount as it leaves. Because the two faces are parallel and there is air on both sides, the emergent ray ends up travelling in precisely the original direction. It has not been turned at all — it has been shifted sideways. That sideways shift is the lateral deviation.
theory.derivationNote: At the first face Snell’s law gives sin i = μ sin r, so the ray bends towards the normal on entering the denser medium. At the second face the ray travels from glass to air and meets the surface at the same angle r, because the faces are parallel and the normals are therefore parallel too. Applying Snell’s law again gives an emergent angle equal to i. The emergent ray is therefore parallel to the incident ray, whatever the angle of incidence and whatever the refractive index — the slab cannot change the direction of the light. Geometry on the path inside the glass gives the perpendicular displacement between the two parallel rays as d = t sin(i − r)/cos r, where t is the thickness of the slab. Two limits are worth noting. At normal incidence i = r = 0, so d = 0 and the ray passes straight through unshifted. As i approaches 90° the expression tends to t itself, so the shift can never exceed the thickness of the slab however obliquely the light strikes it. And since t appears as a simple factor, doubling the thickness doubles the shift.
keyEquations: At the first face: sin i = μ sin r
At the second face the emergent angle equals i, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray
Lateral deviation: d = t sin(i − r) / cos r
At normal incidence d = 0; as i → 90°, d → t
d is directly proportional to the thickness of the slab

apparatus.name: Rectangular glass slab
apparatus.spec: crown, flint or perspex; 1.5 to 4.5 cm thick
apparatus.why: The refracting medium; parallel faces are essential for the emergent ray to be parallel

apparatus.name: Drawing board, paper and pins
apparatus.why: The standard method of tracing the incident and emergent rays

apparatus.name: Protractor
apparatus.why: Measures the angles of incidence and refraction on the traced diagram

apparatus.name: Millimetre scale
apparatus.why: Measures the perpendicular distance between the incident and emergent rays

apparatus.name: Sharp pencil and set square
apparatus.why: For drawing the normal accurately and for measuring the perpendicular displacement

procedure.text: Place the slab on the paper and draw its outline. Mark a normal at the point where the ray will enter.
Set the angle of incidence and fix two pins on the incident ray, well apart.
Look through the opposite face and fix two more pins so that all four appear in one straight line.
Remove the slab and join the pin positions to trace the incident, refracted and emergent rays.
Measure the angle of refraction at the first face with the protractor.
Extend the incident ray forward and measure the perpendicular distance from it to the emergent ray: that is the lateral deviation.
Repeat for at least four widely different angles of incidence, and check each time that the emergent ray is parallel to the incident one.

steps: For each reading compute sin i and sin r
Find μ = sin i / sin r for each, and take the mean
Check that the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray in every case
Plot the lateral shift against the angle of incidence
Confirm that the shift grows with the angle and never exceeds the slab thickness

secondary.quantity: Lateral shift at 45° through a 3 cm slab

expectedResult.statement: The ray bends towards the normal on entering the glass and away from it on leaving, by exactly the same amount, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but displaced sideways. For crown glass μ comes out at about 1.52. The shift grows with the angle of incidence and is directly proportional to the thickness of the slab, but never exceeds that thickness however obliquely the light strikes.

safety: Push the optical pins into the board vertically and never leave them lying loose on the bench.
Handle the glass slab by its edges; a chipped or cracked slab should be reported rather than used.
Do not press the slab hard against the pins, which can snap them.
Keep the working area clear so the board does not slide while the pins are being sighted.
sourcesOfError: The pins not vertical, so the line joining them is not the true path of the ray.
The two pins on each ray placed too close together, which magnifies the angular error in the traced line.
The outline of the slab shifting between placing the pins and tracing the rays.
Parallax when reading the protractor, giving an error of a degree or so in r.
Measuring the shift along the face instead of perpendicular to the rays.
The faces of a cheap slab not being accurately parallel, so the emergent ray is very slightly turned.

viva.question: Why is the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray?
viva.expectedConcept: Because the two faces of the slab are parallel, so the normals at the two faces are parallel too. The ray meets the second face at the same angle r at which it travelled inside the glass, and Snell’s law then gives an emergent angle equal to the original angle of incidence. Same direction, so the rays are parallel.
viva.answerLogic: Parallel faces mean equal angles at entry and exit.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the slab turns the ray permanently through some angle.

viva.question: What is lateral deviation, and what does it depend on?
viva.expectedConcept: It is the perpendicular distance between the incident ray produced forward and the emergent ray — the sideways shift of the beam. It is given by d = t sin(i − r)/cos r, so it depends on the thickness of the slab, the angle of incidence and the refractive index.
viva.commonMisconception: Confusing lateral shift with the angle of deviation in a prism.

viva.question: What happens at normal incidence?
viva.expectedConcept: Nothing at all. With i = 0 Snell’s law gives r = 0, so the ray is not bent at either face and d = t sin(0)/cos(0) = 0. The light passes straight through undeviated and unshifted.
viva.answerLogic: i = 0 gives r = 0 and no shift.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting some shift even along the normal, because the medium has changed.

viva.question: Can the lateral shift ever be larger than the slab thickness?
viva.expectedConcept: No. As the angle of incidence approaches 90°, sin(i − r)/cos r approaches 1, so d approaches t and never exceeds it. The shift is bounded by the thickness of the glass however obliquely the light strikes.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming the shift grows without limit with the angle.

viva.question: How does the shift change if a slab of twice the thickness is used?
viva.expectedConcept: It doubles. The thickness appears as a simple multiplying factor in d = t sin(i − r)/cos r, so at the same angle of incidence and with the same glass, the shift is directly proportional to t.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting the relation to be non-linear because the geometry looks complicated.

viva.question: Why does a glass of higher refractive index give a larger shift?
viva.expectedConcept: Because a larger μ bends the ray further towards the normal, making r smaller for the same i. That increases (i − r), and hence sin(i − r), so the ray travels a more slanted path across the glass and emerges further to one side.
viva.answerLogic: Larger μ means smaller r and a bigger (i − r).
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking μ affects only the direction and not the displacement.

viva.question: Why must the pins be fixed vertically?
viva.expectedConcept: Because the line joining the pin positions on the paper is taken to be the path of the ray. A tilted pin meets the paper at a point that is not directly below its top, so the traced line is displaced from the true ray and both the angle and the shift come out wrong.
viva.answerLogic: A tilted pin marks the wrong point on the paper.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing only the spacing of the pins matters, not their tilt.

viva.question: Why should the two pins on each ray be well separated?
viva.expectedConcept: Because a line is drawn through them, and the angular uncertainty in that line is the position error of the pins divided by their separation. Pins a centimetre apart give a line good to several degrees; pins ten centimetres apart give one ten times better.
viva.answerLogic: A longer baseline gives a better-defined line.
viva.commonMisconception: Placing both pins near the slab so they are easy to sight together.

viva.question: Is any light lost at the surfaces of the slab?
viva.expectedConcept: Yes. At each face part of the light is reflected rather than transmitted, and the fraction reflected grows as the angle of incidence increases. Near grazing incidence most of the light is reflected, which is why the emergent beam becomes faint and hard to locate at large angles.
viva.answerLogic: Partial reflection at each surface, increasing with angle.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming all the light is transmitted because the glass is transparent.

viva.question: Could total internal reflection occur at the second face of the slab?
viva.expectedConcept: No, never, for a parallel-sided slab in air. The ray inside the glass meets the second face at the angle r, and r is always smaller than the critical angle because r itself came from sin i = μ sin r with sin i at most 1. So the ray always emerges.
viva.answerLogic: r can never reach the critical angle in a parallel slab.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting total internal reflection at large angles of incidence.

options: Parallel to the incident ray but displaced
